Cash For Days

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Unscrupulous immigration officers employed by the Department of Home Affairs at the Beitbridge port of entry are working in cahoots with touts and bus drivers in the sale of entry stamps to desperate

Unique Selling Point:
Unscrupulous immigration officers employed by the Department of Home Affairs at the Beitbridge port of
entry are working in cahoots with touts and bus drivers in the sale of entry stamps to desperate travellers
visiting South Africa from Zimbabwe.

Summary:
It happens in two ways:
● those travelling via bus give touts or conductors a total of R400 (R300 is to bribe dodgy border
officials and the R100 for the touts).
● Those travelling by foot put R300 in their passports and the immigration officers take it and give
them a maximum of 90 days.
It is so bad that conductors could have about 20 people in a bus whose have overstayed in the country or
who simply need the full 90 days. All of them give the conductor money

Further information:
For this story, we could spy cam the bus senario and buy days ourselves. We also need to spy cam the sale
of days directly from an official and confront the recently appointed Border Management Agency that
was established to put an end to such problems.

Press Release:


Cash For Days
On a long-distance bus from Pretoria to the Beitbridge Border Post, the conductor makes his passengers an irresistible offer. He can help them extend their stay in South Africa beyond the 90-day legal limit – for a small fee. Many of his passengers are undocumented foreign nationals who should be on their way back to Zimbabwe. Instead, they’ll pay the fee to obtain a new 90-day stamp and “legally” remain in the country. Many of them won't even stand face to face with the customs official who stamps their passports. On these long-distance buses, this practice – called buying days – is common, as bus drivers and Home Affairs officials line their pockets at the expense of those desperate to remain in South Africa. Carte Blanche investigates.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Govan Whittles

1’15” According to immigration laws, residents of other SADC countries are allowed to visit South Africa for a maximum of 90 days per year.
Those who want to stay longer often travel back over the border into Zimbabwe, then return immediately - stamping their passports each way to prove that they have left,and start a new 90-day cycle.
No wonder many have found - that it’s easier to simply pay a bribe.
Tafadzo Jumo is a Zimbabwean national and journalist investigating this trade.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Unscrupulous immigration officers employed by the Department of Home Affairs at the Beitbridge port of entry are working in cahoots with touts and bus drivers in the sale of entry stamps to desperate
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Unscrupulous immigration officers employed by the Department of Home Affairs at the Beitbridge port of entry are working in cahoots with touts and bus drivers in the sale of entry stamps to desperate travellers visiting South Africa from Zimbabwe.
metadata.Summary: It happens in two ways: ● those travelling via bus give touts or conductors a total of R400 (R300 is to bribe dodgy border officials and the R100 for the touts). ● Those travelling by foot put R300 in their passports and the immigration officers take it and give them a maximum of 90 days. It is so bad that conductors could have about 20 people in a bus whose have overstayed in the country or who simply need the full 90 days. All of them give the conductor money
metadata.Further information: For this story, we could spy cam the bus senario and buy days ourselves. We also need to spy cam the sale of days directly from an official and confront the recently appointed Border Management Agency that was established to put an end to such problems.
